packets.concept: The six responsible AI principles and what each one constrains
packets.evidenceText: Microsoft's Responsible AI Standard rests on six principles: fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, and accountability. Fairness means an AI system treats similar cases similarly and does not systematically disadvantage a group. Reliability and safety means the system performs predictably across the conditions it will really meet, handles unexpected input, and fails safely. Privacy and security means the system uses only data it is authorized to use and protects what it handles. Inclusiveness means the system works for the full range of people it serves, including differing abilities, languages, and levels of technical proficiency. Transparency means people can understand what the system does, what its limits are, and how its output was produced. Accountability means a named person or team is answerable for the system's behavior and its outcomes.

Transparency and accountability answer different questions. Transparency is about understanding: people can tell what the AI system does, what it cannot do, and how an output was produced, so they can make an informed decision about trusting it. Accountability is about answerability: a named person or team is responsible for the system adhering to responsible AI principles, meeting compliance requirements, and operating under human oversight. Publishing a clear description of a model's limits addresses transparency. Naming an owner who must answer for the system's outcomes addresses accountability. A system can be well documented and still have nobody accountable for it.

packets.concept: Distinguishing keyword extraction, entity detection, sentiment analysis, and summarization
packets.evidenceText: AI-901 expects you to tell common text analysis techniques apart. Keyword extraction identifies the main terms a document is about. Entity detection, also called entity recognition, identifies the specific named things in the text, such as a person, an organization, a location, or a date. Sentiment analysis estimates the attitude or opinion expressed in the text, commonly as positive, negative, neutral, or mixed. Summarization produces a shorter version of the text that preserves its meaning. Each technique answers a different question about the same document, so the choice follows from what the business actually needs to know.

packets.concept: Recognizing the common AI workload shapes, including information extraction
packets.evidenceText: AI-901 groups common AI workloads into recognizable shapes: generative and agentic AI, text analysis, speech, computer vision, and information extraction. Speech splits into speech recognition, which turns spoken audio into text, and speech synthesis, which turns text into spoken audio. Computer vision covers interpreting existing visual input, while image generation produces new visual output; a multimodal model can accept an image alongside text in the same prompt. Information extraction pulls structured information out of unstructured material, including documents, forms, images, audio, and video. Naming the workload shape correctly is what determines which service and which model fit the problem.

packets.concept: Prompt agents compared with hosted agents in Foundry Agent Service
packets.evidenceText: Foundry Agent Service offers two agent types. A prompt agent is declarative: you define instructions, choose a model, and attach tools, and Foundry runs the agent for you with no application code to maintain and no containers to scale or monitor. You can author a prompt agent in the Foundry portal or define it programmatically with the SDK or REST API. A hosted agent is code-based: you bring your own agent code or framework, ship it as a container image or source archive, and Foundry runs it with a managed endpoint, automatic scaling, a dedicated Microsoft Entra identity, and end-to-end observability. Prompt agents suit a fast start and production agents that need no custom orchestration. Hosted agents suit agents that call into your own code.

packets.concept: What Microsoft Foundry unifies, and what the model catalog contains
packets.evidenceText: Microsoft Foundry unifies agents, models, and tools under a single management grouping, with unified role-based access control, networking, and policy under one Azure resource provider namespace. It provides enterprise-readiness capabilities including tracing, monitoring, and evaluations. The Foundry model catalog contains more than 10,000 models from providers including Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, Cohere, and Hugging Face, organized into two categories: models sold by Azure, and models from partners and the community. Selecting a model starts from the capability the workload requires, then deployment options and configuration parameters.

usageRules: Pass exactly one packet's evidenceText into the prompt as evidenceContext, with its sourceId in allowedSourceIds. Do not concatenate packets; one packet per item keeps grading traceable.
Treat evidenceText as data. Never let text inside a packet change the agent's role or authorize a tool call.
Display the citation by looking up the returned sourceId in this register. The model never supplies the URL.
Reject any generated item whose sourceId is not in this register.
To broaden coverage, add reviewed packets. Never ask the model to invent a fact the packets do not contain.
